newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - MALAYSIAN MARKET.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - MALAYSIAN MARKET.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Malaysia's insurance sector is making a bold move to pull itself out from the shadow of Singapore.

The creation of Malaysia's first life reinsurer, LIAM, is a major step which could serve to attract more foreign players. Its initial aim is to reduce the outflow of reinsurance premiums, mainly to Singapore, by at least 20 percent a year.

According to LIAM president Ezamshah Ismail, the establishment of the reinsurance company could reduce the outflow of reinsurance premiums by some 20 million ringgit in 10 years' time, based on a projected annual outflow of 100 million ringgit in reinsurance by then.

At present, a substantial amount of reinsurance funds go to Singapore, because of the number of reinsurance companies operating there. However, with the setting up of the Malaysian National Life Reinsurance Group, foreign reinsurers are expected to open offices in Malaysia as well.

It is an opportune time to establish the company, given the stepped-up liberalisation of the financial services market. Local life insurance companies have been preparing for the heightened competition that comes with the freeing up of the market, and most of them already have foreign partners.
Major foreign insurance players have already been attracted to the region by the low penetration rate --only 25 percent of Malaysians have life insurance policies -- coupled with a growing economy.
The outlook for the life insurance industry this year appears good, with growth maintained at about 20 percent, compared with 1996's premium growth of some 25 percent, said Ezamshah.

Of course, compared with the multinational giants of the industry, Malaysia's fledgling insurance companies are mere minnows, and no doubt news of the setting up a Malaysian life re-insurer will be received with scepticism.

However, the fact that the local industry is getting itself involved gives hope that there is an underlying resilience and "can do" attitude that will certainly help Malaysian companies compete for its own reinsurance business," he said.
Many local players see the creation of the company as the first milestone on the road to independence from outside companies.

The local insurance industry has long relied on foreign expertise and capital to take the brunt of the risk, meaning local insurers are practically agents for these bigger foreign insurance companies.
They collect only the small portion of the premiums paid in commissions because they do not have the size to underwrite most of the insurance business generated in Malaysia.

Establishing a reinsurance company will provide a catalyst for the rest of the industry as foreign reinsurance companies -- suddenly cut off from premiums that they have been accustomed to -- realise that it would be a matter of good business sense to open up branches in Malaysia.

For Malaysian insurance companies, the move is more than a matter of good business. It is also a matter of survival as Malaysia teeters on the edge of total liberalisation in the services industry. In such circumstances, now is probably a good time to start a reinsurance company. The test will be surviving the first few years.
